title: Recursion Basics
summary: Introduction to methods that call themselves: base case termination, recursive step progression, and stack growth.
subtopics: Recursive Step Moving Toward Base Case
learningOutcomes: Write basic recursive methods for factorial and countdowns
Identify missing base cases that trigger StackOverflowError
Trace the Call Stack growth and unwinding phases of recursion

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Recursion Basics

breakdown.whatIsIt: Comprehensive exploration of Recursion Basics in Java.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Crucial for writing maintainable, reusable, and bug-free Java applications.
howItWorks: Decomposes complex logic into self-contained subprograms.
Allocates local variables on Call Stack frames.
Passes arguments by value, copying parameter data into frames.
Returns execution control back to caller upon reaching return statement.
keyTakeaways: Mastering Recursion Basics is essential for Java placement interviews and clean architecture.
Methods enforce the DRY principle by eliminating redundant duplicate code.
Parameters act as local placeholders; arguments provide runtime values.
Always consider edge cases such as invalid input parameters or stack overflow.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Recursion Basics
activities.description: Watch how stack frames are pushed until n = 1, then resolved in reverse order.

questions.prompt: What are the two mandatory components of every well-formed recursive method?
options: A for loop and a while loop
A base case and a recursive step that moves toward the base case
A try block and a catch block
A static modifier and an int return type
questions.explanation: Every valid recursive function must have a base case to stop recursion, and a recursive step progressing toward that base case.

questions.prompt: What runtime error occurs if a recursive method is missing its base case?
options: java.lang.NullPointerException
java.lang.StackOverflowError
java.lang.ArithmeticException
java.lang.ClassCastException
questions.explanation: Missing a base case causes infinite recursive calls until the Call Stack memory is exhausted, throwing StackOverflowError.

questions.prompt: What happens during the 'unwinding' phase of a recursive algorithm?
options: New stack frames are created for the operating system
Base case has been reached, and paused stack frames pop off the Call Stack, returning values back to their callers
The program restarts from main()
Variables are written to the database
questions.explanation: During unwinding, stack frames pop off in reverse order (LIFO), completing paused expressions using returned values.

questions.prompt: What is the return value of 'sum(3)' given: 'int sum(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n + sum(n - 1); }'?
How does recursion compare to iteration (loops) in terms of memory overhead?
options: Recursion uses zero memory
Recursion incurs memory overhead because each recursive call allocates a new stack frame on the Call Stack
Loops use more stack memory than recursion
Both use the exact same memory in all situations
questions.explanation: Each recursive call consumes a stack frame. Standard loops reuse the same stack frame, making loops more memory efficient.

questions.prompt: Can any problem solved recursively also be solved iteratively with loops?
options: No, recursion has mathematical powers loops can never achieve
Yes, by Church-Turing thesis and computer science principles, any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively (often using an explicit stack)
Only on 64-bit JVMs
Only for sorting algorithms
questions.explanation: All recursive algorithms can theoretically be transformed into iterative equivalents using loops and, if necessary, an explicit stack data structure.

questions.prompt: Given: 'void printNums(int n) { if (n <= 0) return; printNums(n - 1); System.out.print(n + " "); }'. What does printNums(3) print?
options: StackOverflowError
questions.explanation: The recursive call occurs BEFORE the print statement. Calls unwind from 1 to 3, printing '1 2 3 '.

options: Recursion that only runs at the end of the year
A form of recursion where the recursive call is the final statement in the method, with no pending work after it returns
Recursion with two base cases
Recursion that returns void
questions.explanation: In tail recursion, the recursive call is the very last operation executed before returning, allowing certain compilers to optimize stack frames.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between direct and indirect recursion?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Direct recursion occurs when methodA() directly calls methodA(). Indirect recursion occurs when a cycle exists between two or more methods, e.g. methodA() calls methodB(), and methodB() calls methodA().
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What happens if a recursive method has no base case?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Without a base case, the method calls itself infinitely. Stack frames keep accumulating on the Call Stack until JVM memory is exhausted, throwing a java.lang.StackOverflowError.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What are the trade-offs between a recursive solution and an iterative solution?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Recursive solutions are often mathematically elegant, concise, and natural for hierarchical or divide-and-conquer problems (like trees, graphs, merge sort). However, recursion consumes $O(N)$ stack memory for call frames and incurs method call overhead. Iterative solutions use $O(1)$ auxiliary stack space and avoid function invocation overhead.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is the Call Stack depth in recursion?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Call Stack depth refers to the maximum number of simultaneous stack frames pushed onto the stack before the base case is reached and unwinding begins. For factorial(N), the stack depth is $O(N)$.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Why is the naive recursive Fibonacci algorithm (fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)) computationally inefficient?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It has an exponential time complexity of $O(2^N)$ because it repeatedly recomputes the exact same subproblems millions of times. For example, computing fib(5) computes fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times. It can be optimized to $O(N)$ using dynamic programming or iteration.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Does Java support automatic Tail Call Optimization (TCO)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. The standard HotSpot JVM does NOT perform tail call optimization (unlike languages like Scala, Haskell, or Scheme). This design choice was made to preserve complete stack traces for security checks and debugging. As a result, deep tail-recursive methods in Java can still cause StackOverflowError.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: How can you increase the JVM stack size if your recursive algorithm legitimately requires deep recursion?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You can configure the thread stack size using the JVM startup flag '-Xss', e.g., 'java -Xss4m Main' to allocate 4 megabytes per thread stack instead of the default 1MB.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

activities.title: Self-Mastery Checklist
checklist: Recursion: When a method solves a problem by calling a smaller instance of itself.
Base Case: The mandatory stopping condition that terminates recursion without further self-calls.
Recursive Step: The progression that reduces the problem size toward the base case.
Stack Winding & Unwinding: Frames are pushed as calls descend, then resolved and popped in reverse order (LIFO).
StackOverflowError: Thrown when recursive depth exceeds Call Stack memory limit.
